flashcard_questions.q: What is the aim of prediction in tectonic hazard management?
flashcard_questions.a: To give people enough warning to evacuate or take protective action.

flashcard_questions.q: Which instrument placed in the ground detects vibrations and small earthquakes?
Which radioactive gas escaping from the ground can signal an approaching earthquake?
How precisely can GPS technology track the movement of tectonic plates?
How narrow a time window can earthquake prediction currently achieve at best?
How much warning can rising magma give before a volcanic eruption?
Why are most people killed or injured during an earthquake?
flashcard_questions.a: They are hit by or trapped inside buildings that collapse.

flashcard_questions.q: What do rubber shock absorbers do in an earthquake-resistant building?
flashcard_questions.a: They absorb vibrations so the structure moves with the shaking instead of resisting it.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are flexible steel frames preferred to rigid concrete in earthquake zones?
flashcard_questions.a: Steel bends without breaking, whereas rigid concrete cracks.

flashcard_questions.q: What does diagonal cross-bracing protect a building against?
Why can buildings be made earthquake-resistant but never earthquake-proof?
flashcard_questions.a: An extremely powerful earthquake can still damage even the best-designed structures.

flashcard_questions.q: Modern seismometer networks can warn people ____ seconds before the shaking arrives.
Which country sends automatic earthquake alerts to mobile phones across affected regions?
Why are earthquake death tolls usually higher in lower-income countries?
flashcard_questions.a: Cheap unreinforced buildings collapse because the country cannot afford resistant construction.

flashcard_questions.q: Which low-cost planning strategy saves lives where expensive technology is unavailable?
flashcard_questions.a: Educating people in how to respond to a hazard.

notes: 15 cards: 4 strategy-to-example (seismometer, radon, cross-bracing, education), 5 cause-to-consequence (building collapse, steel versus concrete, shock absorbers, wealth and death tolls, resistant not proof), 4 process-to-fact figures (GPS millimetres, two-year window, days or weeks, Japan alerts), 1 cloze on the 10–60 second warning, 1 term-to-purpose card on prediction. Avoided listing the Three Ps as one card because that answer is an enumeration; each P is tested through its own method cards.
